newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy government seen riding out Di Pietro exit.
newsitem.headline: Italy government seen riding out Di Pietro exit.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi is expected to survive the spectacular exit from his government of star anti-graft investigator Antonio Di Pietro who angrily threw in his job as Public Works Minister.

Di Pietro resigned on Thursday after coming under investigation himself for alleged malpractice during his time in the elite team of Milan magistrates that broke the corrupt mould of traditional Italian politics in the early 1990s.
"This is a blow but the government can absorb it and I don't think that this is going to bring about a crisis," Franco Pavoncello, a political scientist, said on Friday.

Cabinet ministers were quick to rebuff opposition calls for Prodi to stand down. "Di Pietro's resignation has shown once more the resilience, seriousness and professionalism of the (government) majority," said Labour Minister Tiziano Treu.

The resignation, which Di Pietro said was irrevocable, comes at a sensitive moment for the government, which is trying to railroad a tough 1997 budget package through parliament in the teeth of bitter opposition.

As if to confirm that it was business as usual, only hours after Di Pietro's exit the lower house of parliament approved the main body of a budget designed to slash 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) from next year's public sector deficit.

"I don't think this is a very strong government, with or without Di Pietro, but the government has so far managed to get its budget through," said John McCarthy, a political science professor at Johns Hopkins University in Bologna.
Di Pietro's shock departure was carried out with the kind of melodramatic flourish which has been a hallmark of his career.

After learning that magistrates were investigating him, Di Pietro wrote to Prodi saying he was the target of a campaign to discredit the celebrated "Tangentopoli" (Bribesville) probes that made his name and shattered the old political order.
He added a signed postscript to the letter pleading with Prodi not to ask him to go back on his decision.
It is not the first time Di Pietro has abandoned public office in a huff.

He quit as a magistrate in December 1994 shortly after the Milan team placed then conservative premier Silvio Berlusconi under investigation for alleged bribery. He has never fully explained why he resigned.
Many of Di Pietro's cabinet colleagues were likely to be happy to see the back of the volatile former magistrate who had public run-ins with Prodi during his time as Public Works Minister.
With the government's immediate future looking secure, attention has turned to what Di Pietro's next move might be.
If Di Pietro, who is still the most popular figure in Italian public life, succeeds in clearing his name he is expected to make a swift return to politics.
"He has raised the stakes. If he emerges unscathed from the investigation his popularity will be double," said Sergio Romano, an ex-diplomat and political commentator.
An opionion poll in the Milan newspaper Corriere della Sera showed 59 percent of those questioned thought Di Pietro was innocent.
Di Pietro and his supporters have portrayed a string of past investigations against him as a vendetta by players in the scandal he exposed.

He was the target of an earlier probe by Brescia magistrates into allegations of corruption and of profiting from holding a public office. All charges against him were dropped in April shortly before Prodi named him to his cabinet.
